cautions: Describe software CATEGORIES and functions generically. Name common examples (e.g., Windows/macOS/Linux; a word processor like Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or LibreOffice Writer) as examples, not as requirements, and never as the only option; reproduce no proprietary UI, icons, or copyrighted screenshots.

Security guidance must reflect CURRENT best practice, which has changed. Follow NIST SP 800-63B: favor long passphrases over forced complexity, do NOT recommend routine periodic password changes (only on evidence of compromise), and screen new passwords against known-breach lists. Recommend a password manager and multifactor authentication (phishing-resistant MFA where possible). Explicitly note where this reverses older advice.

Teach phishing and malware for RECOGNITION and DEFENSE only. Do not provide instructions, code, or techniques for creating malware, phishing kits, or attacks. Frame everything as how to protect oneself and one's organization.

Technical explanations (how the web/DNS/HTTP/TCP work, file systems, storage types) must be accurate and sourced to standards bodies or reputable technical documentation. Distinguish the internet from the web; distinguish RAM (volatile) from storage (non-volatile); distinguish a URL, a domain, and an IP address.

Privacy and security content is educational, not individualized legal or security advice. Represent privacy as involving trade-offs and note that laws (e.g., GDPR, state privacy laws) exist without giving legal advice; do not tell readers they are safe or compliant.
Date any statistic (breach costs, market share, adoption rates) with its year and source; technology figures move quickly.
Distribute question answer keys EVENLY across A/B/C/D, ensuring at least one C and one D per topic; do not single out any position. Verify keys yourself from the file.
